They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there. "Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi. The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI) . Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died. stories.title: South Sudan’s National Election, Its First, Will Be Delayed
stories.summary: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Officials in South Sudan, the world’s youngest state, said on Saturday that its first national election would be postponed, raising new questions about a vote that analysts had already said could not yield a credible result. The National Elections Commission said in a statement that the presidential and legislative elections, which had been scheduled for Dec. 22, would be held on Feb. 11 instead. The country’s information minister, Ateny Wek Ateny, said the postponement would allow more time to register voters and educate them about the process. South Sudan has never held a national election. Since gaining independence from Sudan in 2011 after decades of war, it has been ruled by President Salva Kiir, and it has faced seemingly intractable political difficulties.

stories.title: Nigeria cautions against travel via Ethiopia's main airport due to altitude
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Bole International Airport is a major travel hub By Aleks Phillips Published 14 November 2026 Nigeria's government has cautioned its citizens, in particular those with medical conditions, against travelling via Ethiopia's main airport due to its altitude. The foreign ministry in Abuja said 16 Nigerians with underlying health problems had died this year while transiting through Addis Ababa. The city sits at an altitude of 2,334m (7,657ft) above sea level, making it one of the highest capitals in the world. Bole International Airport is a major hub for travel between Africa, the Middle East and Asia, serving millions of passengers a year. Nigeria said those with cardiovascular and respiratory conditions were at an increased risk.

stories.summary: Publicité En Guinée, après l’expulsion des orpailleurs de Siguiri : "Cette ville ne peut pas tenir sans eux" La décision, début novembre, des autorités guinéennes d’interdire l'orpaillage "anarchique" dans la région de Siguiri, a provoqué le départ de dizaines de milliers d’orpailleurs, en grande partie vers le Mali, et fait éclater des violences le 11 novembre. stories.title: Terror from the skies: drones are redefining warfare in Sudan, and massacring its civilians
stories.summary: View image in fullscreen Terror from the skies: drones are redefining warfare in Sudan, and massacring its civilians Composite: Guardian Design / Getty Images Strikes with huge death tolls are an increasing occurrence as UAVs ‘bring the war to places that were once safe’ The first drone struck the busy transport hub near a market in Al-Dibab as hundreds of people gathered to board trucks to take them back to their homes. Ten minutes later on the evening of 18 October, a second drone hit the same site in the town in West Kordofan state, Sudan . At least 139 people were killed. Eight days after the “double-tap” attack – designed to maximise casualties by killing and injuring emergency responders, volunteers and bystanders on top of the original victims – a drone hit a busy market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur. Emergency Lawyers, a rights group tracking violence in Sudan, put the death toll from that attack at 103. “I lost my 19-year-old son,” a Nyala resident told Agence France-Presse. “We buried him alongside more than 70 bodies in a single site.” View image in fullscreen The remains of Alneam market after a drone strike in the disputed Abyei region along the border between South Sudan and Sudan last month.

stories.title: Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever

Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military's top ranks. stories.summary: ‘I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey’ … Simbarashe Kundizeza View image in fullscreen ‘I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey’ … Simbarashe Kundizeza Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’ The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation. Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter , which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October. Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement : “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.” She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation. “Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.” Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.

The refugee agency said in October alone, around 1,200 people crossed into Diffa and another 3,400 into Tahoua, as violence continued to force families from their homes. stories.title: Kenya Starts Countdown to End of Ebola Outbreak
stories.summary: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Kenya began a countdown on Wednesday to declare the end of its Ebola outbreak. The final patient who had tested positive for the virus was discharged from the hospital on Wednesday. And the Kenyan cabinet secretary for health, Aden Duale, said at a news conference that the last 11 people being monitored for Ebola symptoms had also been discharged after completing a 21-day quarantine period. “For the first time since this outbreak began, Kenya has no patient under treatment and no contact in quarantine,” he said. The milestone is further evidence that countries have succeeded in containing the small number of cases, most coming in from the Democratic Republic of Congo, where the outbreak continues to spread. Since Kenya announced its first-ever Ebola case on Oct. 6, two people have died and nine have tested positive in the country.

stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5PKmp Prefer DW on Google Wael Mohya has the chance to make German football history if he plays under Jürgen Klopp Image: Marvin Ibo Güngör/GES/picture alliance Advertisement If you watch the Bundesliga , then you'll know Wael Mohya is a fast-footed, quick-thinking footballer. But not even the 17-year-old (Mohya turns 18 on December 31) Borussia Mönchengladbach youngster would have expected to be called up to the Germany squad so soon. "Of course, I was absolutely thrilled. It means a great, great deal to me. I think everyone dreams of being selected for the national team at some point," Mohya said. "And the fact that it's come to this now is, of course, just awesome and makes me very proud." Mohya was at the gym when the call came in. He then shared the good news with his parents over dinner. "They started crying," the teenager said in a video posted on Gladbach's social media channels.

stories.title: Shipwreck Off Senegal Kills Dozens as Canary Islands Declare Migrant Emergency
stories.summary: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT On one side of the water, a nation is in mourning. On the other, alarms are sounding. The dueling reactions in Senegal and the Canary Islands came after dozens of Senegalese migrants trying to reach Europe died when their boat capsized last week. Their deaths along one of the world’s riskiest migration routes occurred at a moment when arrivals to Europe are down overall but still overwhelming local officials and dominating the political debate. The Senegalese authorities said on Monday that at least 39 bodies had been recovered off the shore of the West African nation, where stubbornly high unemployment has driven many young men to attempt dangerous sea crossings to Europe in recent years.

stories.title: 'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted
stories.summary: Image caption, Agnes Shikoli says she fears either drowning, or being crushed by her house By Thomas Mukhwana Africa correspondent Published 11 November 2026 "It flooded up to here in March," Agnes Shikoli says, pointing to a spot halfway up the 6ft [1.8m] corrugated iron wall of her home in Kibera, one of the largest informal settlements in Kenya. Her tiny house lies just a couple of metres from the Ngong river, which runs through this densely populated area in the capital, Nairobi. The scars of floods in the long rainy season earlier this year can still be seen - including a broken TV in the corner which was immersed in water. Tucked out of sight is a photo of her sister Beatrice Khalayi, 58, who died when intense rains caused widespread destruction in Kibera. She was among more than 60 people across the country who lost their lives. "Someone called me to tell me that she had died of electrocution after her house flooded," Shikoli recalls. "When I see a picture of her, I feel uneasy, that's why I keep it far from me, so I don't see it." With Kenya's short rainy season now starting, Shikoli tells the BBC she is afraid - especially following warnings that the El NiÃ±o weather phenomenon could bring a new round of flooding. "I feel like it can kill us.

stories.title: Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5PGDc Prefer DW on Google European colonialism was marked by the — often extremely violent — exploitation of people and resources. [Pictured: Clearing of land by setting grass on fire during a German research expedition to Tendaguru in German East Africa, 1909–1913] Image: Archiv/Museum für Naturkunde Advertisement Racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: At first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious. In 1941, Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler himself compared Eastern Europe to "Germany's India" after the British colonial model, declaring that "like the English, we shall rule this empire with a handful of men." But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire, and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared, remains the subject of intense debate. This is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust . Others have argued that the intense focus on the Nazi era has, at least in part, come at the expense of a meaningful reckoning with Germany's colonial history. 'Murder for the very purpose of murder': The industrialized mass murder carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau had no direct precedent in colonial history. [Pictured: Cans of Zyklon B gas, Auschwitz-Birkenau, German Nazi concentration and extermination camp in Poland] Image: Taiftin/Depositphotos/IMAGO "I do think this is nonsense," says Stephan Malinowski, a Professor of Modern European History at the University of Edinburgh. "If it were true, then all other colonial countries who are not discussing the Holocaust, like Great Britain for example, or France or Spain or Portugal, they would then supposedly be very, very attentive to colonial crimes and to colonial history, which it seems to me is not the case." "Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence," a new exhibition at the German Historical Museum in Berlin curated by Malinowski, does not aim to settle the debate but to tell its story. From colonial brutality to Nazi rule The exhibition begins with a hippopotamus-hide whip used in African colonies displayed alongside a canister of Zyklon B, the poison used in Nazi gas chambers.

stories.title: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities
stories.summary: Lewis Hamilton with members of the Egyptian Red Crescent near the Rafah border crossing between Egypt and the Gaza Strip Photograph: Reuters View image in fullscreen Lewis Hamilton with members of the Egyptian Red Crescent near the Rafah border crossing between Egypt and the Gaza Strip Photograph: Reuters Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory. The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire. “I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine . I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October. A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

stories.title: Kenyan Domestic Worker Sentenced to 100 Lashes in Saudi Arabia
stories.summary: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT A Saudi court has sentenced a domestic worker from Kenya to 100 lashes for giving birth outside marriage. The ruling, issued last month, shows the limits of a decade of social and legal reforms in a kingdom where women can be jailed and punished for “illegal pregnancy.” The sentence is a harsh turn in what has been a terrifying ordeal for a mother who has tried for more than a year to return to Kenya with her child but has been blocked at every turn. The mother, Esther Wanja Muthoni, is one of thousands of East African domestic workers who were recruited to work as housekeepers and nannies in Saudi Arabia. A New York Times investigation last year showed how Ms. Muthoni and others wind up trapped in a bureaucratic maze if they become pregnant.

stories.title: Immigrants Are Being Systematically Returned Home Despite Court Orders
stories.summary: Mustapha Camara worked 12-hour shifts during the pandemic as a nurse in Nebraska. In July, ICE agents arrested him in front of his family home. A judge had already prohibited the U.S. government from deporting him to Gambia, where he risked persecution. Here’s how he ended up there anyway. Mustapha Camara and immigrants like him had court protections that they thought made them safe from the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign.

stories.title: U.S. Global Health Strategy Jeopardizes Prevention of Pandemics, Experts Warn
stories.summary: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Country by country, the Trump administration has been negotiating secretive agreements with nations across Africa to provide health aid under strict conditions. The agreements, structured to benefit the United States, are undermining efforts to prepare the world for the next pandemic, putting even Americans at risk, public health experts warn. In one striking example, under an agreement signed in February that was never made public, the United States is set to stop funding health care workers in the Democratic Republic of Congo by the end of the year. Congo has been struggling to contain an Ebola outbreak that has topped 10,000 cases and has spread to two other regions of Africa. The plan, a copy of which was obtained by The New York Times, provides Congo with $900 million over the next five years, and was signed before the Ebola outbreak was detected.

stories.summary: Traumatised by war and stuck in poverty, most of the 400,000 or so Sudanese child refugees now living in Egypt are a generation in limbo, support workers say. Illustration: Patrycja Podkościelny/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Traumatised by war and stuck in poverty, most of the 400,000 or so Sudanese child refugees now living in Egypt are a generation in limbo, support workers say. Illustration: Patrycja Podkościelny/The Guardian Abandoned and traumatised: child refugees at ‘violent’ breaking point in Egypt after fleeing Sudan war Three years of conflict has left hundreds of thousands of Sudanese children out of school and vulnerable to gangs and drugs M ounds of rubbish, the stench of raw sewage and, at night, roaming drug dealers and gangs. These are the streets of a forsaken neighbourhood in Cairo that Sudanese children call home, after fleeing the violence of their country’s civil war . It is here that Tala*, a social worker, spends her days trying to bring deeply traumatised war refugees back from the brink.

stories.title: The legacy of South Africa’s first Black showjumper and his horse-riding school in Soweto
stories.summary: View image in fullscreen The legacy of South Africa’s first Black showjumper and his horse-riding school in Soweto A local BMX rider shows off his skills to Enos Mafokate on an afternoon ride through the streets of Soweto. Photograph: Karabo Mooki Enos Mafokate began his career as a stable hand and went on to become a world-class athlete during the apartheid era. In September 2026, aged 80, Enos died in Johannesburg – but his legacy endures through his horse-riding school and the generations of pupils he inspired In a historically wealthy sport dominated by the white elite and plagued by its colonial reign, a Black athlete draped in a red coat represented his nation. This is the remarkable story of Enos Mafokate and the legacy he worked so hard to create. A professional equestrian rider, Enos began his career as a stable hand and went on to become a world-class athlete during the apartheid era in South Africa .

stories.title: From the streets of Lagos to the Chanel catwalk: how a creative’s thrift-shop style took her to Paris
stories.summary: Rachel Ojuromi models clothes sourced from markets and secondhand shops in her Lagos videos. stories.title: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
stories.summary: People at the scene of the collision in Giza province. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen People at the scene of the collision in Giza province. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said. The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry. An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.

stories.title: 'Devastating message' as ANC records worst-ever result in South Africa election
stories.summary: Image source, EPA Image caption, Voters cast their ballots at a polling station during South Africa's local government elections in Johannesburg By Ed Habershon Reporting from Johannesburg Published 8 November 2026 South Africa's ANC has recorded its worst-ever showing in local elections since Nelson Mandela led the country out of apartheid and into democracy more than 30 years ago, a result the party has called "catastrophic". While it won the most votes of all parties in the country, the African National Congress won 31% of the overall vote, one third down from the 46% it gained in 2021, and a far cry from the 65% 20 years ago. The story of its decline is also clear in the provinces and cities. The party won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo. It also won the most votes in just two of the eight cities, compared with six at the last local elections.

stories.title: Footage shows derailed carriages after fatal train crash in Egypt
stories.summary: Footage shows derailed carriages after fatal train crash in Egypt Footage shows derailed carriages after fatal train crash in Egypt Close A train collision has killed at least seven people and injured dozens in northern Egypt. Footage showed multiple overturned carriages and dozens of people surrounding them. One train was travelling from Giza to the Fayoum oasis, south west of Cairo, while the other was heading from Cairo to Aswan in the south. It is yet unclear what caused the accident but Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said an investigation was underway and would "hold accountable anyone who proves their negligence".
